cells.tense: Right now the practice is steady and you are in it with your whole attention.
cells.ask: Show one piece of the work to someone in your life today, not to be judged and not to be fixed, just so it is in the room with both of you.
cells.core:
You have a rhythm going that doesn't eat you. The repetition is quiet and it's yours, and being alone with it leaves you warmer toward people rather than further from them. You come back to the table with something, and they can feel it.

What makes it hold is that you're refining for its own sake, not to stay ahead of a fear. The good version of this looks like one hour, kept faithfully, and no accounting afterward. Keeping it costs you the stopping: when the hour is done you close the book and walk back into the room. From here the small clear thing this practice has built is free to break something that didn't hold, and it does that best in front of someone.
cells.sheetLine: Your practice feeds the people around you.
cells.verb: keeping a small practice lit on your own time
cells.place: the place in a life where you feel with people and stand alongside them

cells.tense: You are rehearsing for a version of this that hasn't happened and building like it's already late.
cells.ask: Finish one session on purpose, stand up, and spend that same stretch of time doing something ordinary among other people instead.
cells.core:
The practice has turned into proof. Every repetition is checking whether you're still good enough, and stopping feels like falling behind a standard that keeps moving. The hours alone have started to look necessary, so the people who matter get the leftover you, and calling this required has gotten hard to argue with.

What's on the other side is the practice flowing without the clamp, where the quiet hours send you back toward people instead of away from them, and refining is something you do because it grows you, not because you're afraid of what stops if you do. You let the session end because it is finished, not because it failed. You set the tools down when today's work is done, and the day is allowed to close.

cells.tense: The practice sits there unfinished, and you have not been able to keep it going for a long while now.
cells.ask: Pick the smallest fair unit you can name, ten minutes once, put it in the calendar next to something you already do for someone else, and let it end there.
cells.core:
You know how to keep at a thing, and right now you can't. Sitting down with it again feels like stepping into cold water, so a practice that could connect you to people has become one more reason to stay back from them. The willingness isn't gone. It's unspent.

What's needed here is fair calibration: you look at what you put out and what comes back, and you adjust until the proportions are right. A small practice, kept because it is owed no more than that, teaches the plain sense of what's right without the obsessive counting. Start with something you can finish today, and notice who else is in the room when you do.

cells.tense: You are already doing the work and you are telling the story as though it happens to you.
cells.ask: Tell one person about one thing you've gotten good at and how long you've actually been at it, in plain words, without saying it just comes naturally.
cells.core:
The practice is running. You show up, you repeat, you get better, and somewhere in how you describe it the effort goes missing. It arrives as talent, or as just how you are. But the hours are yours, and the people around you have been feeling the result of them: steadier, more aligned, more able to meet them where they are.

The practice is real; the name for it isn't. When you leave the labor out, you also leave out your part in it, and then the refining looks like something that merely happened. Naming it hands the credit back, and it also hands back the simpler earlier version, the doing of the thing before the story about it. One honest sentence about the time you've put in is enough.
